# The Hedging Hump: Why Half-Believing a Tip Is the Worst Thing You Can Do

*A tip about where to look can save you almost all of your work, or cost you more than having no tip at all. Which one you get depends on how much you trust it, and on where the tip points.*

---

## A game of hide and seek with numbers

Here is a simple game. A friend picks two whole numbers, $p$ and $q$, each uniformly at random from $1$ to $M$, and keeps them secret. Your job is to find the **smaller** of the two, $J = \min(p, q)$. You may ask about one number at a time: "Is $J = 17$?" Each question is a *probe*. You keep probing until you hit $J$. What you pay is the number of probes.

This is a toy, but a useful one. It is the simplest model of looking for the smaller of two hidden quantities. The best-known example is the smaller prime factor of a number $N = pq$. Trial division climbs up from the bottom. Fermat's classical method starts at $\sqrt N$ and works from the top. Both are ways of choosing *an order of search*, and the toy game strips that choice down to its bones.

The first observation is that $J$ prefers small values. For $J$ to equal $1$ it is enough that *either* number is $1$. For $J$ to equal $M$, *both* numbers must be $M$. Counting the pairs gives the exact law

$$
\Pr(J = i) = \frac{2(M - i) + 1}{M^2}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, M,
$$

which falls in a straight line from roughly $2/M$ down to $1/M^2$. We will call it the **min-law**.

When the probabilities are known, the best order is obvious, and it is a classical fact (the rearrangement inequality): **probe the most likely values first**. Here that means $1, 2, 3, \dots$ in order. The expected number of probes is then

$$
B(M) = \frac{(M+1)(2M+1)}{6M} \approx \frac{M}{3}.
$$

For $M = 512$ this is $171.17$ probes. Keep that number in mind. It is the price of searching **blind**.

## Enter the oracle

Now suppose someone whispers a tip: *"$J$ is somewhere in this window,"* naming a block of $W$ consecutive cells. Write $x = W/M$ for the fraction of the range the window covers. If the tip were certain, you would search only inside the window and pay at most $W$ probes. That would be a speedup of up to about $1/x$.

Real tips are not certain, though. You might believe this one with some **trust level** $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$. The natural way to act on partial belief goes like this. Put total probability $\alpha$ on the window and $1 - \alpha$ on everything outside it. Inside each part, keep the relative odds the prior already gave you. Concretely, a cell $j$ with prior probability $p_j$ gets the new weight

$$
q_\alpha(j) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\alpha}{P(S)}\, p_j & j \text{ in the window } S,\\[2mm] \dfrac{1-\alpha}{1-P(S)}\, p_j & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
$$

where $P(S)$ is the prior probability that $J$ lies in the window. Then you search in the best order for these new weights, which is again "most likely first." Call the expected cost $E(\alpha)$.

There is one special trust level. If $\alpha = P(S)$, you trust the tip exactly as much as the prior already did. The formula then returns the prior unchanged and $E$ equals the blind cost. We call this the **calibrated** trust. It is the "no news" point.

You would expect the following picture. As trust moves from "ignore the tip" ($\alpha = 0$) to "bet everything on it" ($\alpha = 1$), the cost should change smoothly, maybe in a straight line, and somewhere in between you should do at least as well as blind search.

That picture is wrong.

## The hump

Take $M = 512$ and a window covering the top quarter of the range, the cells $385$ to $512$. Plot $E(\alpha)$ against $\alpha$:

| trust $\alpha$ | expected probes $E(\alpha)$ |
|---|---|
| $0$ (ignore the window entirely) | $154.10$ |
| $0.0625$ (calibrated: no news) | $171.17$ |
| $\approx 0.22$ (**the peak**) | $\approx 196.5$ |
| $1$ (trust the window completely) | $43.17$ |

The curve rises from $154$ through the blind level $171$ to a peak near $196.5$, and then falls steeply to $43$. A searcher who trusts the tip about one-fifth of the way pays **about 15% more than a searcher with no tip at all**. They also pay more than someone who rejects the tip outright, and four and a half times more than someone who believes it fully.

We call this the **hedging hump**. Partial trust is not a safe middle ground. It is the most expensive way to act.

Why does it happen? With weak trust, the searcher still starts at the bottom, at cells $1, 2, 3, \dots$ But the extra weight on the window drags window cells forward in the order, one after another, ahead of low cells that are actually more likely. The searcher ends up with an order that is wrong whichever way the truth falls. If $J$ is small, which is likely, the searcher has wasted probes up at the top. If $J$ is in the window, the searcher has not committed hard enough to reach it quickly. Hedging spreads your effort over two hypotheses and serves neither well.

## Three theorems behind the picture

The striking part is that this is not a quirk of one example. The shape of the curve follows from a few clean facts.

**The curve is always concave and made of straight pieces.** For any fixed order of search, the expected cost is a *linear* function of $\alpha$. The weights $q_\alpha$ depend linearly on $\alpha$, and the cost of a fixed order is a weighted sum of them. The optimal searcher picks the cheapest order at each $\alpha$, so $E(\alpha)$ is the **lower envelope of $M!$ straight lines**. A minimum of lines is always concave and piecewise linear: it can bend downward, never upward. So any interior peak is a genuine summit.

**The hump appears for every decreasing prior.** Here is the general statement.

> **Hedging Hump Theorem.** Let the prior $p_1 > p_2 > \dots > p_n$ be strictly decreasing, and let the window $S$ have prior mass strictly between $0$ and $1$. Suppose the average position of $J$ inside the window differs from its average position outside. Then there is a trust level $\alpha$ strictly between $0$ and $1$ at which the optimal search costs strictly more than searching with no tip.

The idea of the proof fits in a paragraph. At the calibrated trust the weights are the prior itself, and they are *strictly* decreasing. Every gap between neighbouring weights is strictly positive, so a small change in $\alpha$ cannot reverse any of them. Near the calibrated point the optimal order therefore stays "ascending." Along a fixed order the cost is linear in $\alpha$, with slope equal to (average position inside the window) minus (average position outside). That slope is not zero, so moving $\alpha$ a little in the uphill direction strictly raises the cost above the blind value. Nothing in this argument uses the min-law. The hump is universal.

**For the min-law and a window at the top, the hump beats everything.** For the two-number game with the window at the right end, we get more:

> **Right-Window Hump Theorem.** For the min-law and a right-hand window of width $W$ with $3W \le M$, there is a trust level strictly between $0$ and $1$ whose cost is strictly larger than (i) the blind cost, (ii) the cost at full distrust, and (iii) the cost at full trust.

Full distrust searches the outside region in order. Its cost is the average position outside the window, which is below the blind average because the window sits at the top. Full trust scans the window from its right end and costs at most $W$. Since $3W \le M$, that is less than the blind cost of about $M/3$. The hump rises above both.

**And there is a ceiling.** How high can the hump go? For *any* probability vector on $n$ cells, scanning forwards and scanning backwards cost $(n+1)$ in total. The better of the two therefore costs at most $(n+1)/2$:

$$
E(\alpha) \;\le\; \frac{n+1}{2}\quad\text{for every }\alpha.
$$

The uniform distribution reaches this bound. For $M = 512$ the ceiling is $256.5$, so the measured peak of $196.5$ climbs about 30% of the way from the blind level toward the worst case possible. There is also a variant of the model in which the window gets weight $\alpha/W$ per cell, uniformly, rather than in proportion to the prior. In that variant the trust level $\alpha = x$ makes the posterior exactly uniform, and the hump reaches the ceiling exactly.

## Where you point matters as much as how wide

Now set trust to $1$ (a perfectly reliable tip) and ask how much a window of width $W$ helps. The answer depends on **where the window sits**.

Suppose the window starts $d$ cells from the right end, so it covers cells $M-d+1$ to $M-d+W$. Scanning it in ascending order is optimal, because the min-law still decreases inside it. A direct summation gives the **placement law**

$$
E \;=\; \frac{(W+1)\,(6d - 4W + 1)}{6\,(2d - W)}.
$$

This one formula answers every placement question:

* **Right is always best.** Sliding the window to the right strictly lowers the cost, for every width $W \ge 2$.
* **Right windows are miniature copies of the whole game.** Restrict the min-law to its top $W$ cells and rescale. You get exactly the min-law on $W$ cells. Restricting the minimum of two uniform numbers to its upper tail gives the minimum of two smaller uniform numbers. So the right window costs $(W+1)(2W+1)/(6W) \approx W/3$, a third of its width, just as blind search costs a third of $M$.
* **A universal ceiling.** For every placement, the speedup over blind search is at most $M/W = 1/x$. This holds exactly for every finite $M$, not just in a limit.
* **The asymptotic law.** Write $M = kW$ and $d = mW$ with $1 \le m \le k$. As the window grows, the speedup tends to
$$
\frac{k\,(2m-1)}{3m-2}.
$$
A right window ($m=1$) gives $k = 1/x$, the full ceiling. A left window ($m=k$) gives $(2-x)/\big(x(3-2x)\big) \approx 2/(3x)$, and a centered window also gives about $2/(3x)$.

So the same width buys about $1/x$ on the right and only about $2/(3x)$ on the left or in the middle. The right-to-left ratio $(3k-2)/(2k-1)$ approaches $3/2$. Placement is worth a 50% bonus: the same number of cells, used in a better place.

The best cell in our tables is $M = 256$ with a right window of width $16$ ($x = 1/16$). It gives a speedup of $43947/2992 \approx 14.69$, close to its ceiling of $16$.

| window fraction | left | centered | right | ceiling $1/x$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1/64$ | $34.40$ | $34.47$ | $45.78$ | $64$ |
| $1/16$ | $10.20$ | $10.30$ | $14.69$ | $16$ |
| $1/8$ | $5.32$ | $5.42$ | $7.68$ | $8$ |

*Speedups at $M = 256$ with a perfectly trusted window.*

## How sure must you be?

Back to partial trust, now for a left window. Suppose you want a speedup of $5.19$, which is roughly what a perfect $1/8$-window delivers on the left. How much must you trust the tip? Searching window-first, the cost is exactly linear in $\alpha$. At $M = 256$ the threshold is:

* for a window of fraction $1/8$: $\alpha^*$ between $0.995$ and $0.996$;
* for a window of fraction $1/64$: $\alpha^*$ between $0.836$ and $0.837$, drifting toward $0.833$ as $M$ grows.

To get serious gains, the tip must be **narrow and nearly certain**. A broad tip that is merely "likely" does not get there.

## The honesty gate

All of this assumed you could simply *choose* a trust level. In practice a tip comes from somewhere, and an honest source must be **calibrated**. Over many games, the tips it gives, together with how often it gives them, must average back to the prior. Formally, a source fires with probability $r$ and leaves you with beliefs $q$; otherwise it leaves you with $q'$; and

$$
p_j \;=\; r\,q_j + (1-r)\,q'_j \quad\text{for every cell } j.
$$

Two facts about such honest signals follow almost immediately.

> **Value is linear in the firing rate.** Whatever the signal, the expected saving of the optimal searcher who listens to it is at most $r\,(n-1)$ probes.

The reason is short. Fix the order that is best for the "no fire" beliefs $q'$. The searcher who ignores the signal can use that order too. The two searchers differ only on the fraction $r$ of games where the signal fired, and there they differ by at most $n - 1$ probes.

> **Uniform tips are capped by the lightest cell.** If, when it fires, the signal says "$J$ is uniformly spread over the window $S$ with total weight $\alpha$", then $r\alpha/W \le p_j$ for every cell $j$ in the window.

The reason: the "no fire" beliefs cannot be negative, so the prior must already hold at least $r\alpha/W$ at every window cell.

Now put the window on the right, where the min-law is thinnest. The lightest cell is the very last one, with prior probability $1/M^2$. The gate closes:

$$
r\,\alpha \;\le\; \frac{W}{M^2},\qquad \alpha\cdot(\text{expected saving}) \;<\; \frac{W}{M} \;=\; x .
$$

For $M = 512$ and $x = 1/16$, a calibrated uniform tip on the right window can fire at most about $1.2\times 10^{-4}$ of the time at full strength, and it saves less than $1/16$ of a probe on average. Blind search costs $171$ probes. **Honest uniform tips about the top of the range are worthless.** On the left, by contrast, the lightest window cell is about $1000$ times heavier, and the cap is a respectable $r\alpha \le 0.117$.

There is a broader point here. The right window is where a *trusted* tip helps most: it has the $1/x$ ceiling and the self-similar structure. It is also where an *honest* tip can say least, because the calibrated trust of the right window is just its prior mass,

$$
P(\text{right window}) = x^2,
$$

which vanishes quadratically as the window narrows. "Start at $\sqrt N$" is exactly a rightmost-interval commitment. It is a strategy that pays off when you have strong prior reason to believe the answer lies there, and whose honestly calibrated capacity goes to zero.

## Hints that say nothing about "which"

One more remark. In the two-number game there are two different questions you could get help with. *Which* of $p, q$ is the smaller? And *where* is the smaller one? An interval tip of the kind studied here gives no information at all about the first question. By symmetry, the window is equally consistent with "$p$ is smaller" and with "$q$ is smaller." Yet it changes the optimal search order completely. Information about location and information about identity are priced separately. A ceiling on what identity-type hints can buy says nothing about location-type hints.

## Checking the numbers

Several independent checks support these results. For every $M$ from $5$ to $8$, the claim that "most likely first" is optimal was confirmed by brute force over all $M!$ search orders. Simulated searchers drawing from the stated laws reproduce the exact expected costs, within the scatter expected from chance. One such simulation was useful in a less comfortable way. An early version of the calculation had the outside-window mass normalized incorrectly, and a simulated mean landing $72$ standard errors from the "exact" value exposed the slip. It is a reminder that a formula and a simulation catch different kinds of mistakes.

## The moral

Three lessons come out of one small game:

1. **Don't half-believe.** The cost of acting on a tip is concave in your trust, and for any decreasing prior there is a band of partial trust where you do worse than with no tip at all. Either commit or ignore.
2. **Aim where it's thin.** A window placed where the prior is smallest buys the full $1/x$. The same window anywhere else buys only about $2/(3x)$.
3. **But honest tips can't aim there.** Calibration ties a uniform tip's strength to the lightest cell it covers. On the right, that is $1/M^2$, and the tip's value collapses below $x$ probes.

The two-number game is tiny. The tension it shows is general: the places where a hint would help most are often the places where an honest hint has the least to say.

# The Hedging Hump and Placement-Structured Ceilings for Interval Hints in Ordered Search

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

We study a searcher who probes the cells $1, \dots, n$ one at a time, in an order of their choosing, looking for a hidden target $J$ with a known prior. The searcher pays the number of probes. An oracle supplies an *interval hint*, "the target lies in the window $S$," and the searcher trusts it at a level $\alpha\in[0,1]$. We prove three groups of results.

**(I) The hedging hump.** Let $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)$ be the Bayes-optimal expected cost at trust level $\alpha$. It is concave and piecewise linear: it is the lower envelope of $n!$ affine functions. For *every* strictly decreasing prior and every window whose conditional mean position differs from that of its complement, some intermediate trust $\alpha\in(0,1)$ makes the optimal search strictly more expensive than ignoring the hint. For the *min-law* prior of $J=\min(U_1,U_2)$, with $U_1, U_2$ independent and uniform on $\{1,\dots,M\}$, and a right-placed window of width $W\le M/3$, partial trust is strictly worse than no hint, than full distrust and than full trust. No hump exceeds the uniform level $(n+1)/2$.

**(II) Placement-structured ceilings.** With perfect trust, a window of width $W$ whose start lies $d$ cells from the right end costs exactly $(W+1)(6d-4W+1)/\big(6(2d-W)\big)$ probes. Cost strictly decreases as the window moves right. Every placement has speedup at most $M/W=1/x$. Asymptotically the speedup is $k(2m-1)/(3m-2)$ for $M=kW$ and $d=mW$. This gives $1/x$ for right windows, about $2/(3x)$ for left and centered windows, and a right-to-left ratio tending to $3/2$. A right window is self-similar: conditioned on it, the target is again a min-law on $W$ cells.

**(III) The calibration gate.** For a calibrated (truthful) signal, the expected saving is at most $r(n-1)$, where $r$ is the firing rate. A hint that is uniform on its window when it fires satisfies $r\alpha\le W\min_{j\in S}p_j$. Under the min-law with a right window this gives $r\alpha\le W/M^2$ and $\alpha\cdot(\text{saving})<x$. Uniform-given-hit hints of this kind can never produce gains on the scale of the blind cost $\approx M/3$.

All numerical claims are reproduced exactly in rational arithmetic and checked against brute-force enumeration and Monte Carlo simulation.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Ordered search with a prior

Let $J$ be a random target in $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with prior $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$. A *search order* is a permutation $\sigma$ of the cells. The searcher probes $\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots$ until the target is found. If the target is in cell $\sigma(i)$, the cost is $i$. For a nonnegative weight vector $q$ we define

$$
\mathrm{cost}(q,\sigma)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} i\,q_{\sigma(i)},\qquad
\mathrm{opt}(q)=\min_{\sigma}\mathrm{cost}(q,\sigma).
$$

By the rearrangement inequality, the minimum is attained by any order that lists cells in non-increasing weight. When $p$ is non-increasing, the ascending scan $1,2,\dots,n$ is optimal.

### 1.2 The two-number model

The guiding example is the search for the smaller of two hidden numbers. Let $U_1, U_2$ be independent and uniform on $\{1,\dots,M\}$, and let $J=\min(U_1,U_2)$. Counting pairs gives the **min-law**

$$
\Pr(J=i)=\frac{2(M-i)+1}{M^2},\qquad i=1,\dots,M. \tag{1.1}
$$

It is strictly decreasing and sums to $1$. Its mean is

$$
B(M)=\sum_{i=1}^M i\Pr(J=i)=\frac{(M+1)(2M+1)}{6M}\approx\frac M3, \tag{1.2}
$$

and since the law is decreasing, $B(M)$ is also the optimal blind cost. For $M=512$, $B=171.17$; for $M=256$, $B=85.83$.

This model abstracts the search for the smaller factor of a product of two numbers. Trial division searches "from the left," at small candidates first. Fermat's method, "start at $\sqrt N$," commits to the extreme right of the candidate range. In this language, a search heuristic is an order, and a heuristic's implicit belief about where the answer lies is an interval hint.

### 1.3 Interval hints and trust

An oracle names a window $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$. We write $P(S)=\sum_{j\in S}p_j$ and assume $0<P(S)<1$. A searcher who trusts the hint at level $\alpha$ moves total mass $\alpha$ onto $S$ and $1-\alpha$ onto its complement $S^c$, and keeps the prior's relative odds inside each part:

**Definition 1.1 (trust posterior).**
$$
q_\alpha(j)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\alpha}{P(S)}\,p_j,& j\in S,\\[2mm]\dfrac{1-\alpha}{1-P(S)}\,p_j,& j\notin S.\end{cases}
$$
The **trust cost** is $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)=\mathrm{opt}(q_\alpha)$.

Three basic facts follow from the definition. First, $q_\alpha$ is a probability vector for every $\alpha$, with total mass $\alpha+(1-\alpha)=1$. Second, it is affine in $\alpha$:
$$
q_{t\alpha+(1-t)\beta}=t\,q_\alpha+(1-t)\,q_\beta .
$$
Third, at the **calibrated trust** $\alpha=P(S)$ the posterior *equals* the prior. So $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(P(S))$ is the blind cost: calibrated trust is "no news."

We also use the **conditional mean positions**
$$
\mu_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{\sum_{j\in S} j\,p_j}{P(S)},\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{\sum_{j\notin S} j\,p_j}{1-P(S)} .
$$

### 1.4 Windows and placements

For the min-law on $M$ cells, a *window* of width $W$ is a block of consecutive cells, and $x=W/M$ is its *fraction*. A **right** window is $\{M-W+1,\dots,M\}$, a **left** window is $\{1,\dots,W\}$, and a **centered** window starts at about $(M-W)/2+1$. In general we parametrize a window by its distance $d$ from the right end: it occupies the cells $M-d+1,\dots,M-d+W$, with $W\le d\le M$. The *speedup* of a strategy is $B(M)$ divided by its expected cost.

### 1.5 Summary of contributions

1. **Shape of the trust curve** (Theorem 2.1). $E_{\mathrm{opt}}$ is concave and piecewise linear.
2. **Uniform ceiling** (Theorem 2.3). $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)\le(n+1)/2$, with equality for the uniform vector.
3. **Universal hedging hump** (Theorem 3.2). For every strictly decreasing prior, partial trust somewhere in $(0,1)$ is strictly costlier than having no hint.
4. **Min-law right hump** (Theorem 3.3). Partial trust is worse than all three reference strategies.
5. **Placement law** (Theorem 4.1) together with monotonicity, self-similarity, the exact ceiling $1/x$ and the asymptotic law $k(2m-1)/(3m-2)$.
6. **Trust crossings** for the $5.19\times$ target (Theorem 4.7).
7. **Calibration gate** (Theorems 5.2–5.5).

---

## 2. The shape of the trust curve

**Theorem 2.1 (concave piecewise-linear shape).** For every prior $p$ and window $S$, the function $\alpha\mapsto E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)$ is concave on $\mathbb R$. Moreover,
$$
E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)=\min_{\sigma}\Big[\alpha\,\mathrm{cost}(q_1,\sigma)+(1-\alpha)\,\mathrm{cost}(q_0,\sigma)\Big],
$$
a minimum of $n!$ affine functions of $\alpha$.

*Proof.* The cost of a fixed order is linear in the weight vector, so
$\mathrm{cost}(t a+(1-t)b,\sigma)=t\,\mathrm{cost}(a,\sigma)+(1-t)\,\mathrm{cost}(b,\sigma)$. Taking the minimum over $\sigma$ shows that $\mathrm{opt}$ is concave on weight vectors. Composing with the affine map $\alpha\mapsto q_\alpha$ preserves concavity. The displayed formula follows from $q_\alpha=\alpha q_1+(1-\alpha)q_0$. $\square$

**Consequence.** Every local maximum of $E_{\mathrm{opt}}$ on $[0,1]$ is the global maximum, and the curve consists of finitely many linear segments, with breakpoints where two cells swap rank in $q_\alpha$.

**Lemma 2.2 (forward plus backward).** For any weight vector $q$ on $n$ cells, the ascending scan and the descending scan together cost
$$
\mathrm{cost}(q,\mathrm{id})+\mathrm{cost}(q,\mathrm{rev})=(n+1)\sum_j q_j .
$$

*Proof.* Cell $j$ is reached at step $j$ in one scan and at step $n+1-j$ in the other. $\square$

**Theorem 2.3 (uniform ceiling).** For every weight vector $q$, $\mathrm{opt}(q)\le\frac{n+1}{2}\sum_j q_j$. In particular,
$$
E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)\le\frac{n+1}{2}\qquad\text{for every prior, window and trust level}.
$$
The uniform vector $q_j=1/n$ attains this bound, so $(n+1)/2$ is the global maximum of the Bayes cost over probability vectors.

*Proof.* The minimum of two numbers is at most their average; apply Lemma 2.2. For the uniform vector every order costs $\sum_i i/n=(n+1)/2$. $\square$

**Proposition 2.4 (uniform-given-hit hints reach the ceiling).** Consider the alternative hint model in which a trusted window receives *uniform* mass: $q(j)=\alpha/W$ for $j$ in a window of width $W$ and $q(j)=(1-\alpha)/(M-W)$ otherwise, with $0<W<M$. At $\alpha=W/M$ this posterior is exactly uniform, so $\mathrm{opt}=(M+1)/2$, and no trust level exceeds this value.

*Proof.* Substitute $\alpha = W/M$: then $\alpha/W=1/M=(1-\alpha)/(M-W)$. Apply Theorem 2.3. $\square$

So in the uniform-given-hit model the hump reaches the absolute ceiling. In the prior-proportional model it rises above the blind cost but stays below the ceiling.

---

## 3. The hedging hump

### 3.1 Rigidity of the greedy order

**Lemma 3.1 (local rigidity).** Let $p$ be strictly decreasing and $0<P(S)<1$. There is a neighbourhood $N$ of the calibrated trust $P(S)$ such that for every $\alpha\in N$ the posterior $q_\alpha$ is non-increasing in $j$. Hence the ascending scan is Bayes-optimal for $q_\alpha$.

*Proof.* At $\alpha=P(S)$ both scaling factors $\alpha/P(S)$ and $(1-\alpha)/(1-P(S))$ equal $1$. For every pair $i<j$, all four inequalities
$$
\tfrac{1-\alpha}{1-P(S)}p_j<\tfrac{\alpha}{P(S)}p_i,\qquad \tfrac{\alpha}{P(S)}p_j<\tfrac{1-\alpha}{1-P(S)}p_i
$$
(and the trivial same-side ones) hold strictly at $\alpha=P(S)$, because $p_j<p_i$. The two sides depend continuously on $\alpha$, and there are finitely many pairs, so all inequalities persist on a neighbourhood. On that neighbourhood $q_\alpha(j)\le q_\alpha(i)$ for every $i<j$, whichever sides of $S$ the cells $i$ and $j$ lie on. $\square$

### 3.2 The committed cost is linear

The ascending scan has cost
$$
\mathrm{cost}(q_\alpha,\mathrm{id})=\alpha\,\mu_{\mathrm{in}}+(1-\alpha)\,\mu_{\mathrm{out}}, \tag{3.1}
$$
which is linear in $\alpha$ with slope $\mu_{\mathrm{in}}-\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$. At $\alpha=P(S)$ it equals the blind cost.

### 3.3 The universal hump

**Theorem 3.2 (Hedging Hump Theorem).** Let $p$ be strictly decreasing, let $0<P(S)<1$, and suppose $\mu_{\mathrm{in}}\ne\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$. Then there exists $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with
$$
E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)>E_{\mathrm{opt}}(P(S))=\mathrm{opt}(p).
$$
That is, some intermediate trust level makes the optimal search strictly more expensive than searching without the hint.

*Proof.* By Lemma 3.1 there is a neighbourhood $N\subseteq(0,1)$ of $P(S)$ on which $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)=\alpha\mu_{\mathrm{in}}+(1-\alpha)\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$. Since $\mathrm{opt}(p)$ is the same expression at $\alpha=P(S)$,
$$
E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)-\mathrm{opt}(p)=(\alpha-P(S))(\mu_{\mathrm{in}}-\mu_{\mathrm{out}}).
$$
If $\mu_{\mathrm{in}}>\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$, pick $\alpha\in N$ slightly above $P(S)$; if $\mu_{\mathrm{in}}<\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$, pick it slightly below. $\square$

*Interpretation.* Around the calibrated point, the optimal searcher does not change order. It keeps scanning upward, but redistributes probability so that the cells it scans first become less likely. Moving trust toward a window that lies "late" in the order raises the conditional probability of finding the target late, and so raises the cost. For a window sitting high in the range ($\mu_{\mathrm{in}}>\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$), the hump lies *above* the calibrated trust. For a left window it lies *below*. The theorem does not depend on any special feature of the min-law: the hump is universal for strictly decreasing priors.

### 3.4 The min-law, right window: partial trust is the most expensive regime

**Theorem 3.3 (Right-Window Hump Theorem).** Let $p$ be the min-law (1.1) on $M$ cells and $S$ the right window of width $W$ with $0<W$ and $3W\le M$. Then there exists $\alpha\in(0,1)$ such that
$$
E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)>\max\big\{\,\mathrm{opt}(p),\;E_{\mathrm{opt}}(0),\;E_{\mathrm{opt}}(1)\,\big\}.
$$

*Proof.* Every position in $S$ is at least $M-W+1$ and every position outside is at most $M-W$. So $\mu_{\mathrm{in}}\ge M-W+1>M-W\ge\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$. Theorem 3.2 gives $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)>\mathrm{opt}(p)$. It remains to show that both endpoint values lie below the blind cost.

*Full distrust.* The ascending scan is admissible, so $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(0)\le\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$. The blind cost is the mixture $P(S)\mu_{\mathrm{in}}+(1-P(S))\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$ with $\mu_{\mathrm{in}}>\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $P(S)>0$, so $\mu_{\mathrm{out}}<\mathrm{opt}(p)$.

*Full trust.* $q_1$ is supported on $S$. The descending scan reaches every cell of $S$ within $W$ probes, so $E_{\mathrm{opt}}(1)\le W$. Finally, $W<B(M)=(M+1)(2M+1)/(6M)$ whenever $3W\le M$: indeed $6MW\le 2M^2<(M+1)(2M+1)$. $\square$

### 3.5 Numerical profile

We computed exact values on an $\alpha$-grid of step $1/200$, at $M=512$ with $B=171.17$ and ceiling $(M+1)/2=256.5$:

| right, $x=1/2$ | $0.2500$ | $114.28$ | $85.83$ | $197.84$ | $0.435$ |
| left, $x=1/4$ | $0.4375$ | $128.50$ | $61.45$ | $186.37$ | $0.310$ |
| centered, $x=1/4$ | $0.2500$ | $120.50$ | $59.17$ | $176.97$ | $0.335$ |
| right, $x=1/64$ | $0.0002$ | $171.08$ | $3.19$ | $173.76$ | $0.015$ |

Every placement shows a hump above the blind cost, including the cases ($x=1/2$; left and centered windows) not covered by Theorem 3.3. For the right $x=1/4$ window the peak of about $196.5$ (about $196$ on coarser grids) exceeds the blind cost by about $15\%$ and covers about $29\%$ of the distance from the blind cost to the uniform ceiling. For the left window the peak sits below the calibrated trust $0.4375$, as the interpretation of Theorem 3.2 predicts.

---

## 4. Placement-structured ceilings

Throughout this section $\alpha=1$. The searcher knows that $J\in S$ and scans $S$ in ascending order. This is Bayes-optimal, because the min-law conditioned on $S$ is still decreasing.

### 4.1 The placement law

**Theorem 4.1 (Placement Law).** Let the window of width $W\ge1$ occupy cells $M-d+1,\dots,M-d+W$ (so $W\le d\le M$). The expected number of probes is
$$
E(d,W)=\frac{(W+1)\,(6d-4W+1)}{6\,(2d-W)} .
$$

*Proof sketch.* Index the window cells by $r=0,\dots,W-1$. Cell $r$ has prior $\big(2d-1-2r\big)/M^2$. The window mass is
$$
Z=\frac{1}{M^2}\sum_{r=0}^{W-1}(2d-1-2r)=\frac{W(2d-W)}{M^2},
$$
and the positional sum is
$$
N=\frac{1}{M^2}\sum_{r=0}^{W-1}(r+1)(2d-1-2r)=\frac{1}{M^2}\Big[(2d-1)\frac{W(W+1)}{2}-\frac{2(W-1)W(W+1)}{3}\Big]=\frac{W(W+1)(6d-4W+1)}{6M^2}.
$$
The conditional expected position is $N/Z$. $\square$

The formula does not depend on $M$, only on the distance $d$ from the right end. This reflects the translation structure of the min-law, whose density is affine in the distance to the right end.

**Theorem 4.2 (right is cheapest).** For $W\ge2$ and $d'<d$ (window moved right), $E(d',W)<E(d,W)$. For $W=1$ the cost is $1$ at every placement.

*Proof.* Cross-multiplying the two fractions, the sign of the difference is that of
$$
(6d'-4W+1)(2d-W)-(6d-4W+1)(2d'-W)=-2(d-d')(W-1)<0 . \qquad\square
$$

**Theorem 4.3 (self-similarity).** The min-law on $M$ cells, conditioned on the right window of width $W$, is exactly the min-law on $W$ cells:
$$
\frac{\Pr(J=M-W+r)}{W^2/M^2}=\frac{2(W-r)+1}{W^2},\qquad r=1,\dots,W .
$$
The right window has prior mass $W^2/M^2=x^2$, and the right window costs
$$
E(W,W)=\frac{(W+1)(2W+1)}{6W}=B(W).
$$

*Proof.* Direct substitution into (1.1); the mass is $Z$ with $d=W$. $\square$

In words: if both numbers exceed $M-W$, then shifting by $M-W$ makes them independent and uniform on $\{1,\dots,W\}$. The minimum of two uniforms, truncated to its upper tail, is again the minimum of two uniforms. A right-window search is a scaled copy of the blind search, and costs a third of its width.

### 4.2 The exact ceiling

**Theorem 4.4 (universal ceiling).** For every placement, the perfect-trust speedup satisfies
$$
\frac{B(M)}{E(d,W)}\le\frac{M}{W}=\frac1x .
$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 4.2 it suffices to treat $d=W$. Then
$$
\frac{B(M)}{B(W)}=\frac{(M+1)(2M+1)W}{M(W+1)(2W+1)}\le\frac MW
\iff (M+1)(2M+1)W^2\le M^2(W+1)(2W+1).
$$
Expanding, this is $3MW(W-M)+(W^2-M^2)\le0$, which holds for $W\le M$. $\square$

The bound holds exactly at every finite $M$. It is a ceiling, not just a limit.

### 4.3 The asymptotic placement law

**Theorem 4.5 (asymptotic placement law).** Fix integers $1\le m\le k$. Let $M=kW$ and $d=mW$. As $W\to\infty$,
$$
\frac{B(kW)}{E(mW,W)}\longrightarrow\frac{k\,(2m-1)}{3m-2}.
$$

*Proof sketch.* Dividing numerator and denominator by $W^2$,
$$
\frac{B(kW)}{E(mW,W)}=\frac{(k+\tfrac1W)(2k+\tfrac1W)(2m-1)}{k(1+\tfrac1W)\big((6m-4)+\tfrac1W\big)}\to\frac{2k^2(2m-1)}{k(6m-4)} . \qquad\square
$$

**Corollary 4.6 (the three placements).** With $k=1/x$:
* *right* ($m=1$): limit $k=1/x$, the full ceiling;
* *left* ($m=k$): limit $\dfrac{k(2k-1)}{3k-2}=\dfrac{2-x}{x(3-2x)}\to\dfrac{2}{3x}$ as $x \to 0$;
* *centered* ($m\approx k/2$): limit $\approx 2/(3x)$.

For every $m\ge2$ the limit is strictly below $k$, since $k(2m-1)<k(3m-2)$. The right-to-left ratio of limits is $(3k-2)/(2k-1)=(3-2x)/(2-x)$, which tends to $3/2$ as $x\to0$. So placement multiplies what a given width buys by up to $3/2$, from about $2/(3x)$ to $1/x$.

**Table 4.1.** Perfect-trust speedups at $M=256$.

| $x$ | left | centered | right | $1/x$ | $2/(3x)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1/64$ | $34.40$ | $34.47$ | $45.78$ | $64$ | $42.67$ |
| $1/32$ | $19.16$ | $19.25$ | $26.93$ | $32$ | $21.33$ |
| $1/16$ | $10.20$ | $10.30$ | $14.69$ | $16$ | $10.67$ |
| $1/8$ | $5.32$ | $5.42$ | $7.68$ | $8$ | $5.33$ |
| $1/4$ | $2.77$ | $2.88$ | $3.93$ | $4$ | $2.67$ |

**Best cell.** At $M=256$ with a right window of width $16$ ($x=1/16$), the speedup is
$$
\frac{B(256)}{B(16)}=\frac{131841/1536}{561/96}=\frac{43947}{2992}\approx14.688\in(14.68,\,14.69).
$$

### 4.4 Partial trust in a left window: the $5.19\times$ crossing

For a left window of width $W$, the committed (ascending, window-first) scan has exact cost
$$
C(\alpha)=\alpha\,\frac{N_W}{P_W}+(1-\alpha)\,\frac{B(M)-N_W}{1-P_W}, \tag{4.1}
$$
where
$$
P_W=\frac{W(2M-W)}{M^2},\qquad N_W=\frac{W(W+1)}{M^2}\Big(\frac{2M+1}{2}-\frac{2W+1}{3}\Big).
$$
These are the window mass and the window positional sum. Formula (4.1) is (3.1) specialized to the min-law.

**Theorem 4.7 (trust crossings).** Let $M=256$ and let $\mathrm{sp}(\alpha)=B(M)/C(\alpha)$.
* For $x=1/8$ ($W=32$): $\mathrm{sp}(0.995)<5.19<\mathrm{sp}(0.996)$, and $C$ is strictly decreasing in $\alpha$, so the crossing $\alpha^*$ is unique and lies in $(0.995,0.996)$.
* For $x=1/64$ ($W=4$): $\mathrm{sp}(0.836)<5.19<\mathrm{sp}(0.837)$.

*Proof.* Evaluate (4.1) in exact rational arithmetic. The cost is affine in $\alpha$ with negative slope $N_W/P_W-(B-N_W)/(1-P_W)$. $\square$

As $M$ grows, the crossings drift: for $x=1/64$, $\alpha^*=0.8367,0.8344,0.8332$ at $M=256,512,1024$; for $x=1/8$, $\alpha^*=0.9957,0.9935,0.9923$. The continuum value for $x=1/64$ is about $0.832$. The right window with $x=1/64$ already crosses at $0.8332$ at $M=256$. The useful regime is **narrow and near-certain**: a wide window must be trusted almost completely, and even a narrow one needs trust above $0.83$.

---

## 5. The calibration gate

The trust level $\alpha$ has so far been a free parameter. A hint produced by an honest mechanism must be **calibrated**: averaged over the hint's randomness, the posteriors must return the prior.

**Definition 5.1 (calibrated binary signal).** A signal fires with probability $r\in[0,1]$. When it fires the posterior is $q$; otherwise it is $q'$. Both are nonnegative, $q$ sums to $1$, and
$$
p_j=r\,q_j+(1-r)\,q'_j\qquad\text{for all } j. \tag{5.1}
$$
The **expected saving** of the signal is $\mathrm{opt}(p)-\big[r\,\mathrm{opt}(q)+(1-r)\,\mathrm{opt}(q')\big]$.

**Theorem 5.2 (uniform hits are capped by the lightest cell).** Suppose $r\le1$, $q'\ge0$, (5.1) holds, and $q_j=\alpha/W$ for every $j$ in a set $S$ of size $W$. Then
$$
\frac{r\alpha}{W}\le p_j\quad\text{for every } j\in S,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad r\alpha\le W\min_{j\in S}p_j .
$$

*Proof.* $p_j=r\alpha/W+(1-r)q'_j\ge r\alpha/W$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.3 (value of information is linear in the firing rate).** For any calibrated signal on $n$ cells with $r\ge0$,
$$
\mathrm{opt}(p)-\big[r\,\mathrm{opt}(q)+(1-r)\,\mathrm{opt}(q')\big]\le r\,(n-1).
$$

*Proof.* Let $\sigma$ be optimal for $q'$. By linearity of cost in the weights,
$$
\mathrm{opt}(p)\le\mathrm{cost}(p,\sigma)=r\,\mathrm{cost}(q,\sigma)+(1-r)\,\mathrm{opt}(q').
$$
Every order costs at most $n$ on a probability vector, so $\mathrm{cost}(q,\sigma)\le n$. Every order costs at least $1$, so $\mathrm{opt}(q)\ge1$. Subtracting, the saving is at most $r(n-\mathrm{opt}(q))\le r(n-1)$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.4 (the calibration gate, min-law, right window).** Let $p$ be the min-law on $M$ cells and $S$ the right window of width $1\le W\le M$. Suppose a calibrated signal ($0\le r\le1$, $\alpha\ge0$, $q,q'$ as above) is uniform-given-hit on $S$. Then
$$
r\alpha\le\frac{W}{M^2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \alpha\cdot(\text{expected saving})<\frac WM=x .
$$

*Proof.* The lightest cell of $S$ is cell $M$, with prior $1/M^2$. Theorem 5.2 gives the first inequality. Theorem 5.3 then gives
$$
\alpha\cdot\text{saving}\le\alpha r(M-1)\le\frac{W(M-1)}{M^2}<\frac WM. \qquad\square
$$

**Theorem 5.5 (calibrated capacity of the rightmost commitment).** The right window has prior mass exactly $W^2/M^2=x^2$. Hence the calibrated trust of a "start at the right end" commitment is $x^2$, which vanishes quadratically in the window fraction.

*Interpretation.* A uniform-given-hit right hint at full strength ($\alpha=1$) saves fewer than $x$ probes on average, against a blind cost of about $M/3$. For $M=512$ and $x=1/16$: $r\alpha\le 32/512^2\approx1.22\times10^{-4}$, and the saving is below $1/16$ of a probe against $171.17$. An explicit extremal signal, firing at the maximal admissible rate, saves $0.0586$ probes, within the bound $r(M-1)=0.0624$. Uniform-given-hit hints can therefore never reach gains on the scale of magnitude ordering.

The gate is a property of the **lightest** window cell, so it is specific to right placement under a decreasing prior. For the left window with $x=1/16$ at $M=512$, the lightest window cell has mass $(2\cdot480+1)/512^2\approx3.67\times10^{-3}$ and the cap is $r\alpha\le0.117$. That is limited (about $2x(1-x)$ in the continuum) but not negligible.

---

## 6. Algorithms

**Algorithm 6.1 (Bayes-optimal ordered search).** Given weights $q$, sort the cells by non-increasing weight and probe in that order. Cost: $O(n\log n)$. Expected probes: $\sum_i i\,q_{(i)}$, where $q_{(1)}\ge q_{(2)}\ge\cdots$.

**Algorithm 6.2 (trust curve).** For a grid of $\alpha$ values, form $q_\alpha$ and apply Algorithm 6.1. This costs $O(Gn\log n)$ for $G$ grid points. Because $E_{\mathrm{opt}}$ is concave and piecewise linear, the exact curve can also be traced through its breakpoints. These are the values of $\alpha$ where an inside cell and an outside cell tie, $\frac{\alpha}{P(S)}p_i=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-P(S)}p_j$, and there are at most $|S|\cdot|S^c|$ of them.

**Algorithm 6.3 (placement evaluation).** Evaluate $E(d,W)$ from Theorem 4.1 in $O(1)$. The speedup is $B(M)/E(d,W)$.

**Algorithm 6.4 (calibration-gate test).** Given a prior, a window $S$ and a desired $(r,\alpha)$, the uniform-given-hit signal exists iff $r\alpha\le W\min_{j\in S}p_j$. In that case set $q'_j=(p_j-rq_j)/(1-r)$.

---

## 7. Numerical verification

* **Optimality of sorting.** For $M=5,6,7,8$, every left and right window, and a random trust level per window, brute force over all $M!$ orders agrees with Algorithm 6.1. The worst gap is at the level of floating-point round-off (about $10^{-16}$), and zero in exact arithmetic.
* **Placement law.** Formula 4.1 agrees exactly with direct summation for all $1\le W\le M<40$ and all placements.
* **Monte Carlo.** Simulated searchers drawing the target from the stated posteriors reproduce the exact expected costs. Across 40 configurations the largest standardized deviation was $|z|=2.34$, consistent with chance.
* **A caught error.** In an early version of the computation the complement mass was normalized incorrectly. The analytic value looked plausible, but a simulated mean landed at $z=-72$. Exact formulas and simulation catch different kinds of errors, and both are needed.

---

## 8. Discussion

**Hedging is the expensive regime.** Theorems 2.1 and 3.2 together say that the trust curve is a concave tent that, for decreasing priors, always rises above the blind level on one side of the calibrated point. Practically, a searcher who is unsure of a hint should not "partially" act on it. The two endpoints, ignoring the hint or committing to it, bracket the sensible strategies, and for narrow right windows both endpoints beat the blind cost (Theorem 3.3).

**Placement beats width.** Theorem 4.4 caps every window at $1/x$, and the right window comes asymptotically close to the cap. Left and centered windows of the same width only reach about $2/(3x)$. The structural reason is self-similarity (Theorem 4.3). A right window is a scaled copy of the whole problem, so it inherits the factor $1/3$ in "cost $\approx$ width$/3$." A left window covers the region where the prior is nearly flat, and so pays about half its width.

**But honesty closes the right door.** The calibration gate (Theorem 5.4) shows that the placement where a trusted hint helps most is the placement where a calibrated uniform hint can say least. Its capacity is governed by the lightest cell, $1/M^2$, and its calibrated trust is $x^2$. A "start at the right end" heuristic, such as beginning a factor search at $\sqrt N$, is in this language a rightmost-interval commitment whose honestly calibrated capacity tends to $0$.

**Location versus identity.** In the two-number model one can also ask *which* of $U_1,U_2$ is the minimum. An interval hint about the value of $J$ is symmetric in $U_1$ and $U_2$, so it carries zero mutual information about which number is the smaller. Yet it changes the optimal order through its direct correlation with $J$. Ceilings on what "which-number" information can buy therefore do not constrain interval hints. The two kinds of information are priced by orthogonal functionals of the posterior.

---

## 9. Future directions

1. **Exact hump height.** For the min-law and a right window of fraction $x$, determine the continuum peak $\max_\alpha E_{\mathrm{opt}}(\alpha)/M$. We conjecture it equals $\tfrac13+c\,x(1-x)^2+O(x^2)$ for an explicit $c$, with the maximum near $x=1/2$. Writing $E_{\mathrm{opt}}=\int\lambda(s)^2/2\,ds$ in terms of level-set measures, the hump should be exactly the cross term $\int\lambda_{\mathrm{in}}\lambda_{\mathrm{out}}$.
2. **Rigidity radius.** With $\rho=\min_i p_i/p_{i+1}$, we conjecture that the ascending order stays optimal exactly on $\{\alpha:\max(\lambda_{\mathrm{in}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{out}},\lambda_{\mathrm{out}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{in}})\le\rho\}$, where $\lambda_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the two scaling factors. This would make Lemma 3.1 quantitative and give a computable lower bound on the hump height.
3. **Polynomial priors.** For $J=\min(U_1,\dots,U_d)$, self-similarity of the tail should give the right-window ceiling $1/x$ for every $d$, with right/left ratio tending to $(d+1)/d$ (proved here for $d=2$).
4. **Multi-signal hints.** Extend Theorem 5.3 to signals with $K$ outcomes. The natural bound is $\sum_k r_k\,(n-\mathrm{opt}(q_k))$ against a common reference order, giving $O(\sum_k W_k\,p_{\min}(S_k)\,n)$ for uniform-given-hit alphabets such as block partitions.

---

## 10. Conclusion

A single small model, the search for the smaller of two random numbers, already shows three general phenomena of hinted search. The cost of acting on a hint is concave in trust and, for any decreasing prior, peaks above the no-hint cost at partial trust. The value of a perfectly trusted window is set by its placement as much as by its width: the exact ceiling $1/x$ is reached by right windows and missed by a factor approaching $2/3$ elsewhere. Calibration ties a uniform hint's strength to the lightest cell it covers, which closes off the most valuable placement to honest uniform hints.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
The Hedging Hump and Placement-Structured Ceilings -- numerical companion.

Setting.  Two numbers p, q are drawn independently and uniformly from {1, ..., M}.
A searcher wants J = min(p, q) and probes the cells 1, 2, ... in some order; the cost
is the number of probes until J is found.  The prior of J is the "min-law"

    P(J = i + 1) = (2 (M - 1 - i) + 1) / M^2,   i = 0, ..., M - 1,

which is strictly decreasing, so the optimal blind order is ascending, with expected
cost B(M) = (M + 1)(2M + 1) / (6M)   (B(512) = 171.17).

An oracle names a window S of cells.  Trusting it at level alpha means putting mass
alpha on S and 1 - alpha off S, each spread proportionally to the prior.  The
Bayes-optimal searcher probes cells in decreasing posterior order; its expected cost
is E(alpha).

This script reproduces every headline number of the paper with exact rational
arithmetic (fractions.Fraction) wherever that is cheap, and floats elsewhere.
Only the Python standard library is used.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Num = Fraction


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core objects
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def min_law(M: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Prior of J = min(p, q) on cells 0..M-1 (cell i means J = i + 1)."""
    return [Fraction(2 * (M - 1 - i) + 1, M * M) for i in range(M)]


def probe_cost(q: Sequence[Fraction], order: Sequence[int]) -> Fraction:
    """Expected number of probes when the cells are visited in `order`."""
    return sum((Fraction(k + 1) * q[c] for k, c in enumerate(order)), Fraction(0))


def opt_cost(q: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Fraction:
    """Bayes-optimal cost: visit cells in decreasing weight (the rearrangement inequality)."""
    w = sorted(q, reverse=True)
    return sum((Fraction(k + 1) * x for k, x in enumerate(w)), Fraction(0))


def window_mass(p: Sequence[Fraction], S: set[int]) -> Fraction:
    return sum((p[j] for j in S), Fraction(0))


def trust_posterior(p: Sequence[Fraction], S: set[int], alpha: Fraction) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Prior-proportional posterior after trusting 'J in S' at level alpha."""
    P = window_mass(p, S)
    return [(alpha / P if j in S else (1 - alpha) / (1 - P)) * p[j] for j in range(len(p))]


def trust_cost(p: Sequence[Fraction], S: set[int], alpha: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    return opt_cost(trust_posterior(p, S, alpha))


def blind_cost(M: int) -> Fraction:
    return Fraction((M + 1) * (2 * M + 1), 6 * M)


def right_window(M: int, W: int) -> set[int]:
    return set(range(M - W, M))


def left_window(M: int, W: int) -> set[int]:
    return set(range(W))


def centered_window(M: int, W: int) -> set[int]:
    s = (M - W) // 2
    return set(range(s, s + W))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Exhaustive check that sorting is optimal (small M)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_exhaustive_sorting() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("1. Sorting is Bayes-optimal: exhaustive check over all M! orders")
    print("=" * 72)
    rng = random.Random(20260824)
    worst_gap = 0.0
    for M in range(5, 9):
        p = min_law(M)
        for W in range(1, M):
            for S in (right_window(M, W), left_window(M, W)):
                alpha = Fraction(rng.randint(1, 99), 100)
                q = trust_posterior(p, S, alpha)
                brute = min(probe_cost(q, perm) for perm in itertools.permutations(range(M)))
                worst_gap = max(worst_gap, abs(float(brute - opt_cost(q))))
        print(f"  M = {M}: all windows checked")
    print(f"  largest gap between brute force and sorting: {worst_gap:.1e}\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The hedging hump (Theorem A)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hump_curve(M: int, S: set[int], steps: int = 200) -> List[Tuple[float, float]]:
    p = min_law(M)
    return [(k / steps, float(trust_cost(p, S, Fraction(k, steps)))) for k in range(steps + 1)]


def demo_hedging_hump() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("2. The hedging hump: E(alpha) is concave and exceeds the blind cost")
    print("=" * 72)

algorithms.name: Exact Trust-Curve Computation via Breakpoint Enumeration
algorithms.description: Computes the Bayes-optimal expected search cost E_opt(α) for the prior-proportional trust posterior exactly over all α in [0,1]. Since E_opt is the lower envelope of the n! affine functions α ↦ cost(q_α, σ), it is concave and piecewise linear, with breakpoints only where an inside cell and an outside cell tie in posterior weight: α p_i/P(S) = (1−α) p_j/(1−P(S)). Same-side pairs never change relative order. Enumerating the at most |S|·|S^c| breakpoints and evaluating the sorted-order cost at each (O(n log n) per point) yields the entire curve in O(|S||S^c| n log n) exact rational operations; the hump peak is the maximal breakpoint value.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT prior p[1..n], window S
P ← Σ_{j∈S} p_j
BP ← {0, 1}
FOR i ∈ S, j ∉ S:
    a ← p_j P / (p_i (1−P) + p_j P)
    IF 0 < a < 1: BP ← BP ∪ {a}
FOR α ∈ sorted(BP):
    q_j ← (α/P) p_j if j ∈ S else ((1−α)/(1−P)) p_j
    w ← q sorted decreasingly
    E(α) ← Σ_k k · w_k
RETURN piecewise-linear interpolation of (α, E(α)); peak = max E

from __future__ import annotations
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def trust_posterior(p: Sequence[Fraction], window: set[int], alpha: Fraction) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Prior-proportional posterior after trusting 'J in window' at level alpha."""
    P = sum((p[j] for j in window), Fraction(0))
    return [(alpha / P if j in window else (1 - alpha) / (1 - P)) * p[j] for j in range(len(p))]


def optimal_search(q: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Tuple[List[int], Fraction]:
    """Bayes-optimal probe order (most likely first) and its expected cost."""
    order = sorted(range(len(q)), key=lambda j: -q[j])
    cost = sum((Fraction(k + 1) * q[c] for k, c in enumerate(order)), Fraction(0))
    return order, cost


def trust_curve_breakpoints(p: Sequence[Fraction], window: set[int]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Exact breakpoints of the concave piecewise-linear curve E_opt(alpha) in (0, 1):
    the trust levels where an inside cell and an outside cell tie in posterior weight."""
    P = sum((p[j] for j in window), Fraction(0))
    pts = set()
    for i in window:
        for j in range(len(p)):
            if j in window:
                continue
            # alpha p_i / P = (1 - alpha) p_j / (1 - P)
            a = p[j] * P / (p[i] * (1 - P) + p[j] * P)
            if 0 < a < 1:
                pts.add(a)
    return sorted(pts)


def exact_trust_curve(p: Sequence[Fraction], window: set[int]) -> List[Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]]:
    """(alpha, E_opt(alpha)) at 0, every breakpoint and 1; linear in between."""
    alphas = [Fraction(0)] + trust_curve_breakpoints(p, window) + [Fraction(1)]
    return [(a, optimal_search(trust_posterior(p, window, a))[1]) for a in alphas]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    M = 32
    p = [Fraction(2 * (M - 1 - i) + 1, M * M) for i in range(M)]
    S = set(range(M - 8, M))
    curve = exact_trust_curve(p, S)
    peak = max(curve, key=lambda t: t[1])
    print("blind:", float(optimal_search(p)[1]), " peak:", float(peak[1]), "at alpha =", float(peak[0]))

algorithms.description: Evaluates in O(1) the exact expected cost of a perfectly trusted window of width W starting d cells from the right end under the min-law, E(d,W) = (W+1)(6d−4W+1)/(6(2d−W)), obtained from closed-form window sums of an arithmetic-progression prior. The speedup B(M)/E(d,W) with B(M) = (M+1)(2M+1)/(6M) is strictly increasing as the window moves right (cross-difference −2(d−d')(W−1)), never exceeds the exact ceiling M/W, and tends to k(2m−1)/(3m−2) when M = kW and d = mW. The routine also returns the optimal placement (always the right end) by direct comparison.
algorithms.pseudocode:
FUNCTION B(M): RETURN (M+1)(2M+1)/(6M)
FUNCTION E(M, s, W):
    d ← M − s
    RETURN (W+1)(6d − 4W + 1) / (6(2d − W))
FUNCTION speedup(M, s, W): RETURN B(M) / E(M, s, W)
FUNCTION asymptotic(k, m): RETURN k(2m−1)/(3m−2)
FUNCTION best_start(M, W): RETURN argmin_{0≤s≤M−W} E(M, s, W)   // = M − W

algorithms.name: Calibration-Gate Feasibility Test and Extremal Signal Construction
algorithms.description: Decides whether a calibrated binary signal (firing rate r, posterior uniform α/W on a window S when it fires) is consistent with a prior p, using the necessary condition r·α ≤ W·min_{j∈S} p_j from non-negativity of the silent posterior q' = (p − r q)/(1 − r), and constructs (q, q') when feasible. It then computes the signal's exact expected saving opt(p) − [r·opt(q) + (1−r)·opt(q')], which is bounded by r(n−1). Under the min-law with a right window the lightest cell has prior 1/M², so the gate is r·α ≤ W/M² and α·saving < x. Cost: O(n log n) exact rational operations.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT prior p, window S (|S| = W), rate r, coverage α
IF r·α > W · min_{j∈S} p_j: RETURN INFEASIBLE
q_j ← α/W for j ∈ S; q_j ← (1−α) p_j / P(S^c) otherwise
q'_j ← (p_j − r q_j)/(1 − r)
IF any q'_j < 0: RETURN INFEASIBLE
saving ← opt(p) − (r·opt(q) + (1−r)·opt(q'))
ASSERT saving ≤ r(n − 1)
RETURN (q, q', saving)
algorithms.code:
from __future__ import annotations
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple


def opt_cost(q: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Fraction:
    w = sorted(q, reverse=True)
    return sum((Fraction(k + 1) * x for k, x in enumerate(w)), Fraction(0))


def uniform_hint_signal(p: Sequence[Fraction], window: Sequence[int], r: Fraction,
                        alpha: Fraction) -> Optional[Tuple[List[Fraction], List[Fraction]]]:
    """Construct the calibrated uniform-given-hit signal (q, q') with p = r q + (1-r) q',
    q = alpha/W on the window (and the remaining 1-alpha proportional to p off the window),
    or return None if calibration makes it impossible (r alpha > W * min_window p)."""
    W = len(window)
    S = set(window)
    if r * alpha > W * min(p[j] for j in window):
        return None
    out_mass = sum((p[j] for j in range(len(p)) if j not in S), Fraction(0))
    q = [alpha / W if j in S else (1 - alpha) * p[j] / out_mass for j in range(len(p))]
    qp = [(p[j] - r * q[j]) / (1 - r) for j in range(len(p))]
    if any(v < 0 for v in qp):
        return None
    return q, qp


def expected_saving(p: Sequence[Fraction], r: Fraction, q: Sequence[Fraction],
                    qp: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Fraction:
    return opt_cost(p) - (r * opt_cost(q) + (1 - r) * opt_cost(qp))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    M, W = 128, 8
    p = [Fraction(2 * (M - 1 - i) + 1, M * M) for i in range(M)]
    right = list(range(M - W, M))
    r = Fraction(W, M * M)          # the gate value for alpha = 1
    sig = uniform_hint_signal(p, right, r, Fraction(1))
    assert sig is not None
    s = expected_saving(p, r, *sig)
    print("saving:", float(s), "<= r(M-1) =", float(r * (M - 1)), "< x =", W / M)
    assert uniform_hint_signal(p, right, 2 * r, Fraction(1)) is None

"""Hedging hump curves E_opt(alpha) for the min-law, M = 512, several placements."""
from __future__ import annotations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def min_law(M: int) -> np.ndarray:
    i = np.arange(M)
    return (2 * (M - 1 - i) + 1) / M**2


def trust_cost(p: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> float:
    P = p[mask].sum()
    q = np.where(mask, alpha / P, (1 - alpha) / (1 - P)) * p
    w = np.sort(q)[::-1]
    return float(np.dot(np.arange(1, len(w) + 1), w))


def main() -> None:
    M = 512
    p = min_law(M)
    idx = np.arange(M)
    B = (M + 1) * (2 * M + 1) / (6 * M)
    windows = {
        "right, x=1/4": idx >= M - 128,
        "right, x=1/2": idx >= M - 256,
        "left, x=1/4": idx < 128,
        "centered, x=1/4": (idx >= 192) & (idx < 320),
        "right, x=1/64": idx >= M - 8,
    }
    alphas = np.linspace(0, 1, 401)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.5))
    for name, mask in windows.items():
        E = [trust_cost(p, mask, a) for a in alphas]
        k = int(np.argmax(E))
        ax.plot(alphas, E, lw=2, label=f"{name}  (peak {E[k]:.1f} at α={alphas[k]:.2f})")
        ax.plot(alphas[k], E[k], "o", color="black", ms=4)
    ax.axhline(B, ls="--", color="tab:blue", label=f"blind cost B = {B:.2f}")
    ax.axhline((M + 1) / 2, ls=":", color="tab:red", label="uniform ceiling (M+1)/2 = 256.5")
    ax.set_xlabel("trust level α")
    ax.set_ylabel("Bayes-optimal expected probes  E_opt(α)")
    ax.set_title("The hedging hump: partial trust costs more than no hint (min-law, M = 512)")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("hedging_hump.png", dpi=150)
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def placement_cost(d: np.ndarray, W: int) -> np.ndarray:
    return (W + 1) * (6 * d - 4 * W + 1) / (6 * (2 * d - W))


def main() -> None:
    M = 256
    B = (M + 1) * (2 * M + 1) / (6 * M)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))
    ax = axes[0]
    for W, c in ((4, "tab:purple"), (16, "tab:green"), (32, "tab:orange")):
        s = np.arange(0, M - W + 1)
        sp = B / placement_cost(M - s, W)
        rel = s / (M - W)
        ax.plot(rel, sp / (M / W), color=c, lw=2, label=f"W = {W} (x = 1/{M // W})")
    ax.axhline(1.0, ls="--", color="tab:red", label="ceiling 1/x")
    ax.axhline(2 / 3, ls=":", color="grey", label="2/(3x)")

    ax.set_ylabel("speedup / (1/x)")
    ax.set_title(f"Placement law at M = {M}: right is best, and reaches the ceiling")

    ax = axes[1]

"""The calibration gate: maximal hit mass r*alpha of a uniform-given-hit hint, by window placement."""
from __future__ import annotations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def main() -> None:
    M, W = 512, 32
    s = np.arange(0, M - W + 1)
    lightest = (2 * (M - (s + W)) + 1) / M**2      # prior of the last (lightest) window cell
    cap = np.minimum(1.0, W * lightest)
    mass = W * (2 * (M - s) - W) / M**2
    B = (M + 1) * (2 * M + 1) / (6 * M)
    E = (W + 1) * (6 * (M - s) - 4 * W + 1) / (6 * (2 * (M - s) - W))
    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
    ax1.semilogy(s, cap, color="tab:blue", lw=2, label="calibration cap  r·α ≤ W·min_S p")
    ax1.semilogy(s, mass, color="tab:cyan", ls="--", lw=1.5, label="window prior mass (calibrated trust)")
    ax1.set_xlabel("window start s (x = 1/16, M = 512)")
    ax1.set_ylabel("honest capacity (log scale)")
    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
    ax2.plot(s, B / E, color="tab:orange", lw=2, label="perfect-trust speedup")
    ax2.set_ylabel("perfect-trust speedup", color="tab:orange")
    h1, l1 = ax1.get_legend_handles_labels()
    h2, l2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
    ax1.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2, loc="center left", fontsize=8)
    ax1.set_title("Where a trusted hint helps most, an honest uniform hint can say least")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("calibration_gate.png", dpi=150)
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# The Hedging Hump: a guided tour

> **The one-line story.** Acting on a tip you *half*-believe can cost more than having no tip at all; where a tip points matters as much as how narrow it is; and the place where a tip would help most is exactly where an *honest* tip can say least.

## 1. The game

Two numbers $U_1, U_2$ are drawn uniformly from $\{1,\dots,M\}$. You must find the smaller one, $J=\min(U_1,U_2)$, by asking "is it $i$?" one value at a time. Every question costs one probe.

Small values are far more likely: $J=1$ needs only *one* of the numbers to be $1$, while $J=M$ needs *both* to be $M$. Counting pairs gives the **min-law**

$$\Pr(J=i)=\frac{2(M-i)+1}{M^2}.$$

The best blind strategy probes $1,2,3,\dots$ in order (most likely first — the [rearrangement inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rearrangement_inequality)), at an expected cost of

$$B(M)=\frac{(M+1)(2M+1)}{6M}\approx \frac M3,\qquad B(512)=171.17.$$

<details><summary>Why "most likely first" is optimal</summary>

If two cells are probed in the order $a$ then $b$ with $q_a<q_b$, swapping them changes the expected cost by $q_a - q_b<0$. So any order that is not sorted by decreasing probability can be improved by an adjacent swap. This exchange argument is the rearrangement inequality in disguise.
</details>

The game is a toy model for searching for the smaller of two hidden quantities — the smaller prime factor of $N=pq$ being the classic example: trial division searches from the left, Fermat's method *starts at $\sqrt N$*, i.e. at the far right.

## 2. Trusting a tip

An oracle says: *"$J$ lies in the window $S$"* — a block of $W$ consecutive cells, a fraction $x=W/M$ of the range. You trust it at level $\alpha$: total mass $\alpha$ goes on $S$, $1-\alpha$ off it, and within each part the prior's relative odds are kept:

$$q_\alpha(j)=\frac{\alpha}{P(S)}p_j\ (j\in S),\qquad q_\alpha(j)=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-P(S)}p_j\ (j\notin S).$$

At $\alpha=P(S)$ — the **calibrated** trust — nothing changes: you are back to the blind cost. Let $E_{\rm opt}(\alpha)$ be the cost of the best order for $q_\alpha$.

Before reading on, guess: as $\alpha$ goes from $0$ to $1$, what does $E_{\rm opt}$ look like? Now try it.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Set the window to *right, x = 1/4* with $M=512$ and press **jump to peak**. At $\alpha\approx0.22$ the searcher pays about $196.5$ probes — **15% more than no tip at all** — while full trust costs only $43$. Watch the white staircase in the lower panel: as you raise $\alpha$ from the calibrated point, window cells leapfrog ahead of likelier low cells one by one. That is hedging: an order that is wrong whichever way the truth falls.

{{visualization:0}}

## 3. Why the hump must exist

**Concavity.** For a *fixed* order, the expected cost is linear in $\alpha$. The optimal searcher takes the cheapest of the $M!$ orders, so $E_{\rm opt}$ is a lower envelope of lines — **concave and piecewise linear**. Any interior peak is the summit.

<details><summary>Theorem (concave piecewise-linear shape) and proof</summary>

For every prior and window, $E_{\rm opt}(\alpha)=\min_\sigma\big[\alpha\,\mathrm{cost}(q_1,\sigma)+(1-\alpha)\,\mathrm{cost}(q_0,\sigma)\big]$. *Proof:* cost is linear in the weights and $q_\alpha=\alpha q_1+(1-\alpha)q_0$; a minimum of affine functions is concave.
</details>

**Universality.** The hump is not a quirk of the min-law.

> **Hedging Hump Theorem.** If the prior is strictly decreasing, $0<P(S)<1$, and the mean position inside the window differs from the mean position outside, then some $\alpha\in(0,1)$ gives $E_{\rm opt}(\alpha)>$ the no-hint cost.

<details><summary>Proof sketch</summary>

At the calibrated trust the posterior is the prior, whose consecutive gaps are all *strictly* positive. By continuity, on a small neighbourhood of $P(S)$ no two cells swap rank, so the ascending scan stays optimal. Along that scan the cost is $\alpha\mu_{\rm in}+(1-\alpha)\mu_{\rm out}$ — a line with non-zero slope $\mu_{\rm in}-\mu_{\rm out}$. Step a little uphill and the cost exceeds the blind value.
</details>

**Worse than everything.** For the min-law and a right window with $3W\le M$, some partial trust is strictly worse than no hint, than $\alpha=0$, *and* than $\alpha=1$. (Full distrust costs at most $\mu_{\rm out}<B$; full trust costs at most $W<M/3\approx B$.)

**A ceiling.** Scanning forwards plus scanning backwards always costs exactly $n+1$, so the better of the two costs at most $(n+1)/2$: no hump can exceed $256.5$ at $M=512$. In the alternative "uniform-given-hit" hint model the posterior at $\alpha=x$ is exactly uniform and the hump touches this ceiling.

{{algorithm:0}}

## 4. Placement: where you point matters

Now trust the window completely. A window starting $d$ cells from the right end costs exactly

$$E(d,W)=\frac{(W+1)(6d-4W+1)}{6(2d-W)}.$$

{{interactive_demo:1}}

Drag the window from left to right. The speedup climbs monotonically and, at the right end, nearly touches the red line $1/x$.

<details><summary>The four facts behind the curve</summary>

1. **Right is cheapest:** the cross-multiplied difference is $-2(d-d')(W-1)<0$.
2. **Self-similarity:** conditioned on the right window, $J$ is again a min-law on $W$ cells (shift both numbers down by $M-W$), so the right window costs $B(W)\approx W/3$.
3. **Exact ceiling:** $B(M)/E(d,W)\le M/W$ for every placement and every finite $M$ (it reduces to $3MW(W-M)+W^2-M^2\le0$).
4. **Asymptotic law:** with $M=kW$, $d=mW$, the speedup tends to $k(2m-1)/(3m-2)$: $1/x$ on the right, $(2-x)/(x(3-2x))\approx 2/(3x)$ on the left; ratio $\to 3/2$.
</details>

The best cell: $M=256$, right window $W=16$ — speedup $43947/2992\approx 14.69$ against a ceiling of $16$.

{{visualization:1}}

{{algorithm:1}}

**How sure must you be?** For a left window searched window-first, a $5.19\times$ speedup at $M=256$ needs trust $\alpha^*\in(0.995,0.996)$ when $x=1/8$, and $\alpha^*\in(0.836,0.837)$ when $x=1/64$ (drifting to about $0.832$ as $M\to\infty$). Big gains demand tips that are **narrow and nearly certain**.

## 5. The honesty gate

Real tips come from somewhere. A *calibrated* source fires with probability $r$ (leaving beliefs $q$) or stays silent (leaving $q'$), and on average returns the prior: $p=r\,q+(1-r)\,q'$.

> **Value is linear in the firing rate:** expected saving $\le r(n-1)$.
>
> **Uniform tips are capped by the lightest cell:** if $q=\alpha/W$ on $S$, then $r\alpha\le W\min_{j\in S}p_j$.

On the right window the lightest cell is the last one, with mass $1/M^2$. So

$$r\alpha\le\frac{W}{M^2},\qquad \alpha\cdot\text{saving}<x .$$

At $M=512$, $x=1/16$: the tip saves under $1/16$ of a probe against a blind cost of $171$. On the *left* the cap is $0.117$ — a thousand times larger. And the calibrated trust of the right window is just its prior mass, $x^2$.

<details><summary>Proof of the linear value bound</summary>

Let $\sigma$ be optimal for the silent beliefs $q'$. The uninformed searcher can use $\sigma$ too, paying $r\,\mathrm{cost}(q,\sigma)+(1-r)\,\mathrm{opt}(q')$. Since $\mathrm{cost}(q,\sigma)\le n$ and $\mathrm{opt}(q)\ge1$, the informed searcher saves at most $r(n-1)$.
</details>

{{visualization:2}}

{{algorithm:2}}

**The tension in one sentence:** the right window is where a *trusted* tip is worth most ($1/x$, self-similar), and where an *honest* uniform tip is worth least ($1/M^2$ cap, $x^2$ calibrated trust). "Start at $\sqrt N$" is a rightmost commitment whose calibrated capacity tends to zero.

<details><summary>Location versus identity</summary>

A window on the value of $J$ is symmetric in $U_1$ and $U_2$: it carries zero information about *which* number is the smaller. Yet it reshapes the optimal search order. Location information and identity information are priced by different functionals, so a ceiling on one says nothing about the other.
</details>

## 6. Run the numbers yourself

The companion script recomputes everything exactly in rational arithmetic: brute-force optimality of sorting for $M=5$–$8$, the hump table, the placement law, the trust crossings, the calibration gate with an explicit extremal signal, and a Monte Carlo cross-check.

{{demo:0}}

## Where next?

Open questions include the exact height of the hump (conjecturally a cross term $\int\lambda_{\rm in}\lambda_{\rm out}$ of level-set measures), the exact rigidity radius of the greedy order, placement laws for $\min$ of $d$ uniforms (right/left ratio $(d+1)/d$?), and value-of-information bounds for whole alphabets of hints. See the *Future Directions* tab.
